content: English marks the future with helpers,
not with an ending on the verb.
WILL + verb = a decision or promise
made as you speak now:
I will help you.                      Press 1
GOING TO + verb = a plan you already
have: We are going to win.            Press 2
'll is spoken will: I'll help.        Press 3
won't = will not, its parts hidden.
Your language may show the future in
its own way; English uses these two.
A modal is a helper verb. It adds
meaning to the plain verb after it.
One rule for the whole family:
modal + base verb - no -s, no -ed, no to.
She can drive. You should sleep.      Press 1
can, could = able to
should = advice
must = no choice
may, might = maybe, possible
would = softer, less direct
They ask and deny with no do:
Can you help? I can't.                Press 2
A look-alike word in your language
rarely maps to a modal one-to-one.

pronunciation_mappings.1: She can drive. You should sleep.

content: The same modals do polite work.
A softer modal makes a gentler ask.
Can I...? asks for permission:
Can I go now?                         Press 1
Could you...? and Would you...? make
a request, softer than can:
Could you help me? Would you wait?    Press 2
Can you explain that? asks, politely,
to hear it again.
please slips in and softens even more:
Could you please wait?                Press 3
Your language may soften with special
forms; English uses the modal itself.

pronunciation_mappings.2: Could you help me? Would you wait?

content: English is written in two standards:
British (UK) and American (US).
Both are correct English.
This pack shows the US spelling by default:
honor, color, center, favorite.
The UK twin adds or moves letters:
honour, colour, centre, favourite.
Install the British voice and every card
switches to UK spelling, spoken as written.
A few whole words differ too:
lorry / truck, film / movie.
Your language may have its own two
standards; if not, here both are right.
English compares in two ways, and the
adjective's length picks which.
SHORT words add -er:
old → older,  big → bigger
(some short words double a final letter:
big → bigger, hot → hotter)
LONGER words take more in front:
important → more important
than names the other thing:
A city is bigger than a house.
A friend is more important than a game.
Many languages use ONE pattern for all.
English uses two — length decides.
The top of the ladder is the
superlative — and the goes with it.
SHORT words add -est:
old → the oldest
LONGER words take the most:
important → the most important
the is always part of the frame:
This is the biggest city of all.
Four wild ones change shape — learn
them whole, like irregular pasts:
good → better → best
bad  → worse  → worst
Your language has its own top form;
here it is -est or most, plus the.
An adjective describes a thing. Add
-ly and it describes an ACTION — how
something is done:
quick → quickly                     Press 1
serious → seriously                 Press 2
A set of -ly words turns up the volume
on what you say: completely, totally,
definitely, certainly, seriously.
I completely forgot.
Watch out — a few adverbs wear no -ly.
fast and hard already do the job:
She runs fast. He works hard.
In English the base how-word tool is
-ly; your language does it its own way.
